# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is associated with a substantial risk of cardioembolic stroke, the majority of which originates in the left atrial appendage (LAA). In a landmark surgical series, of the 1288 patients with non-rheumatic atrial fibrillation involved in their study, 221 (17%) had thrombus detected in the left atrium, and the overwhelming majority of these thrombi were localized to the appendage [1]. This anatomical observation provided the conceptual basis for mechanically excluding the LAA from the circulation as an alternative to lifelong oral anticoagulation (OAC). Although OAC with vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) and, more recently, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) is highly effective, a substantial proportion of patients have contraindications, bleeding complications, or poor adherence, motivating the development of percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC) [2].

## Pivotal randomized evidence with the Watchman device

The first randomized trial, PROTECT AF, compared the Watchman device with warfarin. The multicenter PROTECT AF study was conducted to determine whether percutaneous left atrial appendage closure with a filter device (Watchman) was noninferior to warfarin for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation; patients (n=707) with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and at least 1 risk factor were randomized to either the Watchman device (n=463) or continued warfarin (n=244) in a 2:1 ratio [3]. The efficacy of percutaneous closure of the LAA with this device was non-inferior to that of warfarin therapy, although there was a higher rate of adverse safety events in the intervention group, mainly as a result of periprocedural complications [4]. Longer-term follow-up [5] and a subsequent extended randomized analysis [6] reinforced these findings.

Because of periprocedural safety concerns, a confirmatory trial, PREVAIL, was performed. At 18 months, the rate of the first coprimary efficacy endpoint (composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular/unexplained death) did not achieve the prespecified criteria for noninferiority, although early safety events occurred in 2.2% of the Watchman arm, significantly lower than in PROTECT AF, satisfying the pre-specified safety performance goal [7]. A patient-level meta-analysis of both trials supported LAAC as a reasonable alternative [8], and a vital-status analysis examined mortality effects [9].

The most mature data come from pooled 5-year outcomes. These 5-year outcomes demonstrate that LAAC with Watchman provides stroke prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation comparable to warfarin, with additional reductions in major bleeding, particularly hemorrhagic stroke [10]. A net clinical benefit analysis found that the upfront risk of periprocedural events is counterbalanced over time by reduced bleeding events and mortality [11].

## Patients ineligible for anticoagulation

A key population comprises patients with contraindications to OAC, who were excluded from the pivotal trials. The observational ASAP study assessed the safety and efficacy of left atrial appendage closure in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation patients ineligible for warfarin therapy, in whom history of hemorrhagic/bleeding tendencies (93%) was the most common reason for warfarin ineligibility [12]. Bleeding outcomes were also characterized in pooled analyses of the randomized experience [13].

## Next-generation devices and comparative trials

Device technology has evolved considerably. The PINNACLE FLX trial evaluated the Watchman FLX; the primary safety endpoint was met with a low adverse event rate of 0.5%, the primary effectiveness endpoint was met with a 100% rate of effective LAA closure at 12 months with peridevice flow < 5 mm, and the implant success rate was 98.8% [14], with sustained 2-year results [15]. The Amulet IDE trial provided the first head-to-head randomized comparison; the Amulet occluder was noninferior for safety and effectiveness of stroke prevention compared with the Watchman device and superior for LAA occlusion, although procedure-related complications were higher with the Amulet occluder and decreased with operator experience [16]. These differences persisted in 3-year [17] and 5-year [18] follow-up, and the SWISS-APERO trial provided additional comparative data [19].

## Comparison with DOACs and integration with ablation

Critically, the pivotal trials compared LAAC only with warfarin. PRAGUE-17 was the first randomized comparison with DOACs. PRAGUE-17 was a multicenter, randomized, noninferiority trial comparing LAAC with DOACs, enrolling patients with nonvalvular AF indicated for anticoagulation who had a history of bleeding, a cardioembolic event while on OAC, and/or a CHA2DS2-VASc of ≥3 and HAS-BLED of >2 [20]. In long-term follow-up, LAAC remained noninferior to DOACs for preventing major cardiovascular, neurological, or bleeding events, and nonprocedural bleeding was significantly reduced with LAAC [21]. The original short-term PRAGUE-17 results established initial noninferiority [22].

More recently, the OPTION trial examined LAAC integrated with AF ablation. LAAC in patients at moderate to high risk for stroke undergoing catheter AF ablation resulted in significantly less bleeding compared with oral anticoagulation [23], and the trial design and subanalyses have further explored concomitant versus sequential strategies [24] and the influence on AF recurrence [25]. A 2025 meta-analysis integrating these data offers a comprehensive long-term comparison [26].

## Real-world data and complications

Registry data confirm broad applicability. In the NCDR LAAO Registry, patients were older and higher-risk, with a mean CHA2DS2-VASc score of 4.6 and a mean HAS-BLED score of 3, yet in-hospital major adverse events related to the procedure occurred in 2.1% of patients, and overall in-hospital mortality was low (0.19%) [27], with an accompanying editorial contextualizing these findings [28]. Outcomes with the Watchman FLX in everyday practice have been similarly reassuring [29].

A persistent concern is device-related thrombus (DRT). A meta-analysis concluded that DRT after LAAO is uncommon (3.8%) but is associated with a 4- to 5-fold increase in ischemic events [30].

## Conclusion

Percutaneous LAAC has matured from an investigational concept into an established therapy for stroke prevention in AF, particularly for patients with contraindications to or complications from long-term anticoagulation. Randomized data support noninferiority to both warfarin and DOACs with reduced long-term bleeding, while next-generation devices and integration with ablation continue to refine outcomes. Residual challenges—device-related thrombus, peridevice leak, and the need for direct comparisons against contemporary DOACs in lower-risk populations—remain active areas of investigation.
